items.prompt: Match each piece of equipment to what it measures.
hints: Each tool measures one kind of quantity.
Think about the units each tool shows: °C, N, seconds, ml or cm.
Start with the stopwatch. Think about what you use it for in a race.
items.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature, a forcemeter measures force and a stopwatch measures time. A measuring cylinder measures the volume of a liquid, and a ruler measures length.

items.prompt: In a fair test, how many variables should you change?

options.why: If you change two things, you cannot tell which one caused the result.
If you change everything, you cannot tell what made the difference.
You need to change one thing to see what effect it has.

hints: A fair test finds out what effect one thing has.
Think about racing two toy cars. Decide what would make the race unfair.
Cross out the choices that would mix up the cause of the result.
items.explanation: In a fair test you change only one variable and keep the others the same. Then any difference in the results must be caused by the one thing you changed.

items.prompt: Sari tests whether the temperature of water changes how fast sugar dissolves. What should she change?

options.why: Keep the amount of sugar the same, so the test is fair.
Keep the cup size the same, so only one thing changes.
The spoon does not matter here, so keep it the same.

hints: Her question tells you what Sari wants to find out.
The variable she changes is the one named in her question.
Read her question again and underline the variable she is testing.
items.explanation: Sari wants to know about the temperature of the water, so that is the variable she changes. She keeps the amount of sugar, the cup and the stirring the same.

items.prompt: Budi tests whether more water makes bean plants grow taller. Sort each variable into the right group.
hints: There is one variable to change and one to measure. Everything else stays the same.
His question names the variable he changes and the result he measures.
Start with the variable named first in his question.
items.explanation: Budi changes the amount of water and measures the height of the plants. He keeps the seeds, soil, pot and light the same, so the test is fair.

items.prompt: Tomás times a paper helicopter falling three times: 2.4 s, 2.6 s and 2.5 s. What is the mean time?
hints: The mean is a kind of average.
Add up all the times, then divide by how many times there are.
Start by adding the three times together.
items.explanation: 2.4 + 2.6 + 2.5 = 7.5, and 7.5 ÷ 3 = 2.5. The mean time is 2.5 seconds.

solution.say: There are three times, so divide the total by 3.

items.prompt: Yuki rolls a toy car down the same ramp four times. Which result does not fit the pattern?

figure.caption: Distance the car rolled
head: Trial
Distance (cm)
figure.alt: Table of results: trial 1, 30 cm; trial 2, 31 cm; trial 3, 52 cm; trial 4, 29 cm.

options.why: 30 cm is close to the other results.
31 cm is close to the other results.
29 cm is close to the other results.

hints: In a good test, repeated results should be close to each other.
Look for the one result that is far away from the rest.
Compare each distance with 30 cm.
items.explanation: Trials 1, 2 and 4 are all about 30 cm, but trial 3 is 52 cm. This anomalous result should be checked by repeating the trial.

items.prompt: Before her test, Wulan writes that ice will melt fastest on the metal tray, because metal conducts heat well. What has Wulan written?

options.why: A conclusion comes after the test, from the results.
Results are the measurements you make during the test.
She has not listed any equipment.

hints: Look at when Wulan wrote this: before or after the test.
She says what she thinks will happen and gives a reason.
Cross out the choices that can only be written after the test.
items.explanation: Wulan says what she thinks will happen before testing, and she gives a scientific reason. That is a prediction with a reason.

items.prompt: Aditya tests which ball bounces highest. He drops a tennis ball from 1 m and a rubber ball from 2 m. Why is his test unfair?

options.why: Changing the type of ball is the point of the test. The drop height should stay the same.

options.text: He did not use a thermometer.
options.why: Temperature is not part of this test.

options.text: He should have used heavier balls.
options.why: The mass of the balls is not the problem. Two variables were changed.

options.text: He changed the drop height as well as the type of ball.

hints: Find the one variable Aditya wants to test.
Check whether anything else changed between the two drops.
Compare the heights each ball was dropped from.
items.explanation: The test is unfair because he changed the drop height as well as the type of ball. He should drop both balls from the same height.

items.prompt: Plan a fair test to find which material makes the best umbrella. Say what you will change, what you will measure and what you will keep the same.

criteria.label: Names the variable to change: the type of material
Says what to measure and how, for example water through in 1 minute
Lists at least two variables to keep the same
Mentions repeating the test or a safety point

planning: How will you measure which material keeps water out best?
What must stay the same for every material?
items.model: I will test four materials: cotton, plastic, paper and wool. I will stretch each one over a cup and pour 50 ml of water on it. I will use a measuring cylinder to measure how much water drips into the cup after one minute. I will keep the amount of water, the size of the material and the time the same. I will repeat each test three times.
hints: Start with the one thing you will change.
Think of a way to measure how much water gets through each material.
items.explanation: A fair umbrella test changes only the material and measures how much water gets through. Everything else stays the same, and repeating the test makes the results more reliable.

items.prompt: Leo puts sugar in Cup A with hot water and stirs it. He puts sugar in Cup B with cold water and does not stir it. The sugar in Cup A dissolves faster. Leo says stirring makes sugar dissolve faster. Why is his conclusion not reliable?

options.text: He changed two variables, so he cannot tell which one made the difference.

options.why: Stirring does help, but this test cannot show it, because the temperature changed too.

options.text: He should have used salt instead.
options.why: Using salt would not fix the problem of changing two things at once.

options.text: He did not use enough sugar.
options.why: The amount of sugar is not the problem. Two variables were changed.

hints: List every difference between Cup A and Cup B.
If two things are different, either one could have caused the result.
Count how many variables Leo changed between the two cups.
items.explanation: Leo changed both the temperature and the stirring, so either one could have made Cup A faster. To test stirring, he must keep the water temperature the same in both cups.

items.prompt: Sari tests how fast ice melts. Label the things she uses.

figure.alt: Four pieces of equipment in a row: an ice cube, a thermometer, a clock and a spoon.

hints: Tap a label, then tap its number.
The thermometer measures temperature.
The clock measures time.
items.explanation: She uses a thermometer for temperature and a clock for time. She uses a spoon to put the ice in the water. The ice cube is what she tests.

items.prompt: Amara grows bean plants with different hours of light. Label what each box is in her fair test.

figure.alt: Three boxes. The top box says hours of light 2, 4 or 6. The middle box says height of the plant in centimetres. The bottom box says same soil, pot and water.

hints: Tap a label, then tap its number.
The thing that is different in each plant is what we change.
The height is what we measure to see the effect.
items.explanation: She changes the hours of light, measures the height and keeps the soil, pot and water the same.

items.prompt: Tomás drops a ball five times and records the height of the bounce. Tap the result that does not fit the pattern.

figure.alt: A bar chart with five bars for trials 1 to 5. Trials 1, 2, 3 and 5 are tall and about the same. Trial 4 is much shorter than the others.

hints: Find the bars that are about the same.
Look for the bar that stands out.
One bar is much shorter than the others.
items.explanation: Trial 4 is much lower than the other four. It is an anomalous result, so he should check it and maybe repeat it.

items.prompt: Dewi wants to find out if light affects plant growth. All pots are the same size with the same soil. Tap the pair that makes a fair test.

figure.alt: Four rows, each showing a pair of pots. Row 1: both in sun, 100 ml and 50 ml of water. Row 2: sun with 100 ml and shade with 50 ml. Row 3: sun with 100 ml and shade with 100 ml. Row 4: a bean in sun and a cress plant in shade.

hints: Only the light should be different.
Check that the water and the plant are the same.
Look for the pair where light changes and nothing else does.
items.explanation: Only the light changes in this pair. The water and the type of plant are the same, so any difference is due to light.

items.prompt: Rangga drops four balls from 1 m and measures each bounce three times. Work out the mean bounce for each ball.
head: Ball
Trial 1 (cm)
Trial 2 (cm)
Trial 3 (cm)
Mean (cm)

Add the three bounces first.
Rubber: 80 + 76 + 78 = 234. Now divide by 3.

items.prompt: Kofi wants to know if light affects how tall a plant grows. Which two plants in the table can he compare for a fair test?

head: Plant
Light
Water (ml)
Pot
figure.alt: Table of four plants. A: sun, 100 ml, small pot. B: shade, 100 ml, small pot. C: shade, 50 ml, small pot. D: sun, 100 ml, large pot.

options.why: Both light and water are different, so we cannot tell which caused a change.
Only the pot size differs, so this does not test light.
Only the water differs, so this does not test light.

hints: The only thing that changes should be the light.
Compare each pair row by row.
Which two plants differ in light but match in water and pot?
items.explanation: Plants A and B differ only in light. Their water and pot size are the same.

items.prompt: Putri melts identical ice cubes in four places. Which conclusion does the bar chart support?

figure.alt: Bar chart of the time for an ice cube to melt: shade 45 minutes, window 30, sunny yard 18, warm tray 9.

options.text: Ice melts fastest in the shade.
options.why: The shade bar is the tallest, so it took the longest.

options.text: The size of the ice cube controls the melting time.
options.why: All ice cubes were the same size, so the size did not change.

options.text: The warmer the place, the faster the ice cube melted.
The tray is a light source, so the ice melted.
options.why: The data tell us about warmth, not about light sources.

hints: Short bars mean fast melting.
Compare the places from coolest to warmest.
What do the shortest bars have in common?
items.explanation: The ice melted in 9 minutes on the warm tray and 45 minutes in the shade. More warmth gives faster melting.

items.prompt: Use the bar chart. How many minutes longer did the ice cube take to melt in the shade than on the warm tray?

figure.alt: Bar chart of the time for an ice cube to melt: shade 45 minutes, window 30, sunny yard 18, warm tray 9.

hints: Read the shade bar and the warm tray bar.
Subtract the smaller number from the larger one.
The shade bar is at 45 minutes.
items.explanation: 45 - 9 = 36 minutes longer.

items.prompt: Hadi times how long a toy takes to fall: 12.1 s, 11.9 s, 17.8 s and 12.0 s. He decides the 17.8 s result is anomalous and leaves it out. What is the mean of the other three results?
hints: First write down only the three results that fit the pattern.
Add them up, then divide by 3.

items.prompt: A helicopter takes 3.2 s, 3.4 s, 3.1 s, 3.3 s and 3.5 s to fall in five trials. What is the mean time?
hints: Mean = total divided by number of trials.
Add all five times first.
The total is 16.5 s. How many trials were there?

items.prompt: A result that does not fit the pattern of the other results is called an ___ result.
hints: It is a result that looks odd.
It might be caused by a mistake.
It begins with the letter a.
items.explanation: An anomalous result does not fit the pattern. We should check it or repeat the test.

items.prompt: In a fair test, you change one thing and keep everything else the ___.
hints: Only one variable changes.
The others must not change.
The word is the opposite of different.
items.explanation: To make a test fair, we keep all the other variables the same.

items.prompt: Put the steps of a scientific investigation in order.
hints: You begin with a question.
Predictions come before the test.
The conclusion comes last.
items.explanation: We ask a question, predict, plan, collect results and then use them to draw a conclusion.

items.prompt: Linh tests which paper towel soaks up the most water. Match each part of her test to its job.
pairs: Size of towel and water poured
hints: The thing you change is the thing you are testing.
What tells you which towel is best?
Repeating helps spot odd results.
items.explanation: She changes the towel, measures the water absorbed and keeps other things the same. Repeats make results more reliable.

items.prompt: Leo tests which ball bounces highest. Sort each variable.
hints: Which variable is different for each ball?
The bounce height is the result.
Everything else should not change.
items.explanation: He changes the ball, measures the bounce height and keeps the drop height, floor and ruler the same.

items.prompt: Choose all the things that make results more reliable.

options.text: Check any odd result by testing again.
Take the mean of the repeats.

options.why: Changing two things makes the results unclear.
One trial could be a mistake. Repeats show whether results agree.

hints: Reliable results agree when you repeat them.
A mean smooths out small differences.
Cross out the ideas that make the test less careful.
items.explanation: Repeating, checking odd results and using a mean all make the results more reliable.

items.prompt: Naya times a car down a ramp once and writes her conclusion. What is the best improvement?

options.text: Use a different ramp each time.
options.why: This changes a variable and makes the test unfair.

options.text: Repeat the test several times and find the mean.

options.why: Ignoring other results is not fair.
The conclusion comes after the results.

hints: One result could be a mistake.
What can she do to check?
More trials help spot odd results.
items.explanation: Repeating the test and taking a mean makes the results more reliable.

items.prompt: Which prediction is best for a test on whether the colour of a drink affects how fast ice melts?

options.text: The colour of the drink will not change how fast ice melts, because colour does not change the temperature.
The ice will melt in 10 minutes.
options.why: This is a guess and gives no reason.

options.text: It will melt because ice melts.
options.why: This does not mention the colour.

options.text: I think red drinks are best.
options.why: This does not say what will happen to the ice.

hints: A good prediction says what you think will happen.
It gives a reason.
It must mention the variable being tested.
items.explanation: A good prediction says what will happen and why, using what we already know.

items.prompt: Budi gives bean plants different amounts of water each day. Which conclusion is best supported by the data?

figure.alt: Bar chart of plant height after different amounts of water: 0 ml 6 cm, 50 ml 14 cm, 100 ml 22 cm, 150 ml 26 cm, 200 ml 18 cm.

options.text: The more water a plant gets, the taller it grows.
options.why: The 200 ml plant was shorter than the 150 ml plant.

options.text: Water has no effect on how tall plants grow.
options.why: The plants with no water were the shortest.
The 150 ml plant was taller, so this is not the best amount.

options.text: Plants grew taller with more water up to 150 ml, but 200 ml was worse than 150 ml.

hints: Read every bar.
Look at what happens after 150 ml.
Check each conclusion against the numbers.
items.explanation: Height rises from 0 ml to 150 ml, then falls at 200 ml. Too much water may harm the plant.

items.prompt: Kofi tests whether warm water dissolves salt faster. He puts 1 spoon of salt in 100 ml of warm water and 2 spoons of salt in 100 ml of cold water. What must he change?

options.why: This would change the water amount, which should be the same.

options.text: Use warm water in both cups.
options.why: Then the temperature would not change.

options.text: Use the same amount of salt in both cups.

options.why: Stirring should be the same in both cups.

hints: Find the two things that are different.
One is the temperature, which he is testing.
What other thing differs between the cups?
items.explanation: He changed the amount of salt as well as the temperature. The salt must be the same in both cups.

items.prompt: Look at the jug. How much water is in it?

figure.alt: A jug with a scale from 0 to 500 ml. Water fills the jug part of the way up.

hints: Look at the level of the water.
Read the nearest mark on the scale.
Each mark is 50 ml.
items.explanation: The water is at the 350 ml mark.

items.prompt: True or false: In a fair test you should change only one variable.
hints: How many things should change?
Others stay the same.
Change just one.
items.explanation: Changing one thing at a time shows what causes any difference.

items.prompt: True or false: If you repeat a test, you should use a different method each time.
hints: Why repeat?
Is the same method needed?
Same method each time.
items.explanation: Repeating with the same method checks that results are reliable. A different method would make comparing harder.

items.prompt: True or false: The thing you measure in a fair test is called the dependent variable.
hints: What do you measure?
Which variable changes as a result?
Measure the dependent variable.
items.explanation: It depends on the change you make, so you measure it to see the effect.

items.prompt: True or false: If a test is fair, you do not need to measure anything.
hints: Can you compare without numbers?
What do you record?
You measure the outcome.
items.explanation: A fair test needs measurements to compare the results, using the right equipment and units.
